title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Trends in floating kelp extent at locations, woven together with other information sources, produce a starkly contrasting assessment of floating kelp status in different sub-basins of Washington State (Figure 4). Generally, sub-basins near oceanic influences show stability (i.e., the North Coast and Strait of Juan de Fuca), while substantial documented declines have been detected in the innermost sub-basins (i.e., Central Puget Sound and South Puget Sound). In other areas, data limitations preclude definitive classification. In sub-basins with limited data, two are identified as areas of concern for decline (i.e., San Juan Islands and Saratoga/Whidbey), while two are identified as having insufficient data without major flags for concern (i.e., North Puget Sound and Admiralty Inlet). Within each sub-basin, long-term trends at specific locations are diverse, demonstrating some local exceptions to the prevailing pattern.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 9 Appendix A contains individual summaries for each sub-basin. Key findings: • Data availability is uneven for assessing floating kelp across sub-basins. Within four sub-basins (of nine with floating kelp), definitive assessments were precluded by data limitations. • Along the North Olympic Coast and Strait of Juan de Fuca, the majority of locations show no longterm trend or increasing trends over decades. As a result, the North Coast (NCO), Western Strait of Juan de Fuca (WST) and Eastern Strait of Juan de Fuca (EST) are considered stable. Some locations showed statistically significant increasing trends. It is important to note that conditions during the early years strongly influence statistical trend test results.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: • In contrast to overall stable conditions In the Eastern Strait of Juan de Fuca (EST), major losses occurred in the eastern portion along Miller Peninsula, Protection Island, and Cape George. • Central and South Puget Sound have experienced substantial documented declines. Monitoring data from a small number of locations included evidence of declines and total losses. These spatially and temporally limited datasets were augmented with historical ecology studies over a century time scale and longer. These historical studies indicate that floating kelp has disappeared from approximately 63-80% of the shorelines (relative to cumulative maximum extent). • There is substantial concern that floating kelp has declined in the San Juan Islands, based on Indigenous Scientific Knowledge and other reports.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: • Total loss of floating kelp occurred along some shorelines at the entrance to Possession Sound, which leads to concern about the state of floating kelp in Saratoga/Whidbey sub-basin. However, data limitations preclude definitive assessment. • In Admiralty Inlet and North Puget Sound, spatial and temporal data limitations preclude assessment. Monitoring results at a limited number of locations did not raise major concerns. The sub-basin status assessment broadly identifies scientific and management priorities at the sub-basins scale. Where floating kelp is stable, conservation is a priority. Where substantial declines occurred, stressor abatement and restoration are priorities. Areas with insufficient data need increased monitoring.

text: 11 Three sub-basins are classified as “Stable”, two as “Concern”, two as “Decline”, two as “Insufficient Data”, and two as “No Floating Kelp” (Table 2). Relative proportions of floating kelp within each status category vary based on which metric is being used (i.e., total nearshore extent, total linear extent, or proportion of statewide floating kelp within each category). Approximately two-thirds of statewide floating kelp bed area in WA is stable (Table 3, “Stable”), approximately one-third has data gaps limiting definitive assessment (Table 3, “Concern” and “Insufficient Data”), approximately one-fifth of floating kelp is either concern or documented decline (Table 3, “Concern”, “Decline”). However, when total linear extent is considered, only 15% of linear extent is classified as “Stable”, while nearly half of linear extent is classified as “Concern” or “Decline”.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: This comparison between metrics is important, because while statewide floating kelp bed area is reassuring (i.e., 67% is “Stable”), total linear extent is much worse (i.e., 15% is “Stable”, while 49% is “Concern” or “Decline”). While it is encouraging that the areas with the largest floating kelp populations are currently stable, loss of floating kelp across large swaths of coastline (e.g., South and Central Puget Sound) likely threaten migration corridors of associated species, floating kelp population connectivity, and resilience of nearshore ecosystems. The observed losses may be modest in terms of total area of kelp beds lost, but much more significant in terms of the total area of kelp range, or area with shorelines that support kelp.

text: Furthermore, these estimates do not account for floating kelp losses that occurred before consistent nearshore monitoring began, which could alter estimates of loss and historical floating kelp distribution. Between the 2022 and the 2023 WA Floating Kelp Vital Sign Indicator reports, two new sites were added to the analysis as their data records reached the five years required for trend assessment (Table 4). Both sites are surveyed by MRCs, and one is located in North Puget Sound (Point Whitehorn) while the other is located in the Saratoga Whidbey sub-basin (Hoypus Point). The newly added sites were both classified as ‘no trend’. In 2023, there were five additional ‘increasing’ site classifications, seven fewer ‘no trend’ site classifications, three additional ‘decreasing’ site classifications, and one additional ‘total loss’ site classification compared to the 2022 assessment (Table 4).

text: 12 Discussion The indicator shows a general pattern in Washington State; concern about floating kelp loss increases with distance from the coast into Puget Sound. Multiple natural and human factors that impact kelp could be contributing to observed patterns. Floating kelps experience a natural high degree of variability in abundance on inter-annual and decadal scales. This variability is often linked to fluctuations in water temperature via large-scale climate oscillations (Pfister et al., 2018). Other stressors include water turbidity, sedimentation, algal epiphytes, water column nutrients, and grazers (Hollarsmith et al., 2022). Sea urchins are known for their ability to completely denude kelp beds in other regions; however, this phenomenon has not been observed at a large scale in Washington State. Other grazers, such as kelp crabs (Pugettia producta) and Lacuna spp.

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: snails may exert stronger grazing pressure, especially in areas with moderate waves and currents. Sea star wasting disease may have decreased natural predation levels on some grazers (Schultz et al., 2016; Menge et al., 2016; Rogers-Bennett and Catton, 2019; Eisaguirre et al., 2020). The global ocean is warming due to the thermal impacts of greenhouse gases (IPCC, 2022), and some coastal regions, including the Salish Sea, are warming more rapidly (Riche et al., 2014, Khangaonkar et al., 2019). Increasing water temperatures and climate change are major emerging concerns for floating kelp in Washington State. In many regions within the northeast Pacific, including Washington State, floating kelp populations dropped around 2014 during a marine heatwave.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Floating kelp recovery in Washington State was spatially complex, with faster recovery at sites closer to oceanic influence and slower or no recovery further inland (Claar et al. in review). Along the North Coast and Strait of Juan de Fuca, total floating kelp extent rebounded in 2015. In contrast, recovery was delayed until 2017 at Cherry Point in North Puget Sound. At some sites in inner basins, total losses were observed, and beds have not recovered (such as Mukilteo in Saratoga Passage and Devil’s Head in South Puget Sound). Declines have continued at Fox Island, and only one kelp individual was observed at that site in 2023. Thermal stress may co-occur with or interact with other stressors, including low nutrients.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: In some areas of Puget Sound during recent years, elevated water temperatures and low nutrient concentrations approached thresholds associated with decreased physiological performance and reproductive success in kelps (Hurd et al., 2014; Muth et al., 2019; Berry et al., 2021; Khangaonkar et al., 2021). However, longterm data on these parameters is lacking, so spatial and temporal patterns in temperature and nutrient concentrations are not well understood. At the time of this Indicator release, a collaborative project is currently underway to better understand spatial and temporal variability in environmental conditions at 15 sites of loss and persistence. That study, funded by the Habitat Strategic Initiative Lead (HSIL), also includes floating kelp mapping and measurements of morphometrics and condition.

title: The Kelp Forest Monitoring Alliance of Washington State: State Summary
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: By integrating those data with ongoing monitoring efforts, we aim to improve our understanding of kelp resilience and loss in the greater Puget Sound. This is the third iteration of the statewide assessment of floating kelp, produced with existing data in order to address pressing needs for greater understanding of status and trends. We believe that the assessment reliably identifies broad patterns in floating kelp abundance and distribution. It also creates a model for weaving together diverse information sources in a holistic approach to synthesizing floating kelp data. Future monitoring will be devoted to further developing our understanding and linking findings to research, restoration, and conservation actions.

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 4 Executive Summary Bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana) forms ﬂoating kelp forests along Washington’s nearshore environment, providing ecologically, economically, and culturally valuable habitat. These dynamic ecosystems are persistent in some regions of the State but have substantially declined in others (Pﬁster et al., 2018, Berry et al. 2021), prompting collaborative regional efforts to study, conserve, and restore bull kelp populations, including the Puget Sound Kelp Conservation and Recovery Plan (Calloway et al. 2020, Whitty et al. 2023), the Washington State Kelp and Eelgrass Health and Conservation Plan (RCW 79.135.440) the Washington State Floating Kelp Indicator (Berry et al. 2022, Claar et al. 2025b). This report presents recommendations developed from one such effort, the 2023-2026 Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: This project was led by the Washington State Department of Natural Resources Nearshore Habitat Program (WDNR), University of Washington Friday Harbor Labs (FHL), and University of Chicago, and was supported by a collaborative team of organizations and individuals who provided valuable data, insight, and guidance. Drawing on intensive ﬁeld sampling at 15 sites throughout the Washington portion of the southern Salish Sea in conjunction with long-term aerial kelp monitoring and other existing datasets, the project examined patterns of bull kelp resilience and loss in relation to environmental conditions, benthic communities and composition, and bull kelp morphology, condition, and performance. This project also functioned as a pilot effort for a large-scale intensive monitoring program.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: We collected datasets at an unprecedented spatial scale and temporal resolution, building on existing monitoring methods and developing new ones. This recommendations report synthesizes insights gained from this intensive effort to guide the design of future bull kelp and environmental monitoring programs that are scientiﬁcally robust, scalable to available resources, and responsive to management needs, with the overarching goal of improving conservation and recovery of kelp forests in the greater Puget Sound region. The monitoring strategy detailed in this report encompasses continuation of and improvements to currently existing monitoring programs led by WDNR and partners (see Claar et al. 2025b), as well as recommendations for new efforts to ﬁll critical knowledge gaps.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: While some elements of this strategy fall within existing monitoring programs that are currently staffed and funded, maintaining and expanding efforts will require continued funding for essential functions and additional investments to conduct monitoring and answer targeted questions. Our core recommendation is to implement a monitoring framework that prioritizes essential measurements at a network of sites while allowing ﬂexibility to expand monitoring and address emerging research and management questions as capacity and

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 5 funding allow. This framework leverages multi-organization efforts to diversify the types of data that can be collected and to increase the feasibility of monitoring across broad spatial and temporal scales. It is not intended to supplant existing programs but rather provide a strategic framework to support and expand collaborative kelp monitoring efforts throughout Washington. Recommendations • Continue annual surface kelp bed monitoring to track changes in kelp bed area as part of the Floating Kelp Vital Sign Indicator and pair site-level surveys with regionalscale kelp bed monitoring (e.g., ﬁxed-wing aerial imagery) to contextualize local changes within a broader spatial extent. Employ a ‘mosaic approach’ to kelp bed monitoring, so that the survey type (e.g., kayak, Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS), ﬁxed-wing aircraft) matches the bed type (e.g., narrow vs. wide).

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 6 I. Purpose of this report The report presents a framework and recommendations for future monitoring of bull kelp populations and associated environmental conditions based on ﬁndings from the 20232026 Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project. Long-term monitoring is essential to the management and recovery of kelp forests in Washington State (Calloway et al. 2020). Monitoring data are used to identify status and trends in kelp forests in the Washington State Floating Kelp Bed Area Indicator (Berry et al. 2022). Efforts like the Washington State Kelp and Eelgrass Health and Conservation Plan (RCW 79.135.440) rely on monitoring data to identify priority sites and strategies for conservation. Monitoring also lays the foundation for targeted, manipulative research by establishing expected conditions that kelp may experience.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: These conditions can then be manipulated in the lab or in the ﬁeld in an ecologically meaningful way, offering insights into the mechanisms of stressors and drivers of kelp distribution. Long-term monitoring programs can identify patterns, track ecological changes, and lay the conceptual foundation for targeted research, and therefore both are critical components of effective and adaptive management. Designing monitoring programs is challenging, because at the outset it is often difficult to know which parameters will be important to detect change. Many questions arise regarding the frequency and timing of sampling and the relative value of any particular measurement compared to others. By integrating knowledge gained from intensive ﬁeld sampling and analysis during the Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project, this report aims to help answer these questions.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: It identiﬁes some guiding principles and priority-ranked monitoring recommendations that will meet our broader goal of informing conservation and management of kelp forests. In Washington State, kelp management, conservation, and recovery are being advanced by a diverse constellation of Tribal, local, state, federal, nonproﬁt, academic, and community groups (e.g., see the Washington Kelp Project Inventory1). The recommendations presented here are not a prescription for all of these groups, but rather a framework for continued collaboration. By synthesizing what we learned in this project, we hope to lay out recommendations that can be leveraged by WDNR and other groups and programs to support future collaborative efforts and development of robust and diverse funding sources for vital long-term monitoring programs. 1 https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/98d08e52caef4e36859c792dfa3bae12

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 7 II. A Monitoring Framework 1. Deﬁning Goals Monitoring programs may be created to answer speciﬁc questions (e.g., is temperature increasing at this location?), to gather baseline data to detect future anomalies and change, or to monitor effectiveness of management actions. Monitoring programs can also reveal patterns connected to resilience and loss, supporting focused hypothesis generation and evaluation. Effective monitoring programs focus on answering identiﬁed questions while supporting ﬂexibility to respond to new research or management needs. To prioritize monitoring of Washington State kelp forests, we discuss the results of the Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project in the context of developing a tiered monitoring strategy and present considerations for prioritizing monitoring tasks and sites.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Washington State already has a robust collection of partners who monitor bull kelp and related conditions and species. The primary goal of this monitoring framework is to support these ongoing partnerships and deepen understanding of trends in canopy-forming kelp. 2. Multi-organizational structure A core component of the Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project was the collaborative nature of data collection. Each partner brought unique expertise, staff, equipment, and capacity, enabling data collection on a range of parameters across a wide spatial scale. Although it requires additional coordination, leveraging the capacity and expertise of diverse partners adds signiﬁcant value to monitoring programs.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: For example, partnering with UW FHL made benthic surveying by scientiﬁc divers possible, while researchers at the University of Chicago brought equipment and expertise that enabled data collection on kelp physiology and performance, and WDNR staff were able to collect monthly water samples and provide previous monitoring data of kelp bed area and environmental conditions. These data streams would have been extremely difficult to collect by any partner organization alone. Concurrent data collection (i.e., more people on the water in more places) multiplied the amount of data collected, accelerating our ability to build linkages among multiple data types. Our recommendations here can be implemented by multiple organizations as capacity and funding allows. 3. Tiered monitoring strategy All of the parameters in the study have demonstrated utility in kelp research. Here, we prioritize their utility for implementation in regional monitoring of kelp forests and

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 8 environmental conditions. This tiered strategy will allow for ﬂexibility in relation to capacity and funding. For all monitoring programs, tasks can be divided up into three tiers of priority: 1. Tier 1: Essential for basic tracking. These provide the bare minimum information required to track system changes at a basic level. They have demonstrated linkages to bull kelp resilience and have well-developed methodology. For example, monitoring ﬂoating kelp bed area over time is key for reporting the status and trends of ﬂoating kelp across Washington. 2. Tier 2: Essential for contextualizing patterns of loss and resilience. These answer questions that can guide future monitoring strategy and/or answer pressing scientiﬁc or management questions. They provide important additional context to Tier 1 tasks.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: These are strategic growth opportunities that may also reveal tasks that need to be elevated to Tier 1. For example, monitoring ﬂoating kelp morphometric parameters, such as sub-bulb diameter and reproductivity, has revealed patterns linked to loss and resilience beyond trends in bed area. While morphometric data can take more relative effort to collect than bed area and may not be needed at every monitoring site, they nonetheless provide insight important for conservation and management. 3. Tier 3: Essential for identifying future research topics and answering targeted questions in local or intensive studies, but not necessarily priority for deploying programmatically at a large scale at this time due to feasibility of data collection. Parameters may be locally important.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: These can test speciﬁc hypotheses, pilot the collection of new types of data, or leverage existing but potentially costly survey methods. These may help answer fundamental scientiﬁc questions that support Tier 1 and Tier 2 tasks. For example, Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Particulate Organic Matter (POM) can provide information about light availability, sedimentation and/or plankton abundance, and are therefore candidates for focused studies at individual sites. However, more research is needed to understand linkages with bull kelp and other environmental factors before integrating into widespread annual monitoring research. Considerations for prioritization of different monitoring tasks include: • Relevance of ﬁndings to identify and describe kelp loss and resilience.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: For example, kelp abundance is clearly important for tracking loss and persistence, and temperature data has demonstrated linkages to kelp loss. • Cost to obtain the data, both in terms of equipment, maintenance, and materials required, as well as staff time to acquire a statistically valid or robust sample size across space and time. In this report, we represent ‘Relative Cost’

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 9 estimates (low, medium, high) to encompass cost and effort relative to data utility or relevance based on data collection experiences from this project. • Frequency of sampling, considering temporal variability of kelp bed area, condition, and performance, as well as environmental and benthic conditions. • Development of the methodology and reliability of the data. For example, some sensors are known to be highly subject to fouling, equipment failure, or drift (e.g., PAR sensors, some deployed salinity sensors) while others are more reliable (e.g., temperature sensors).

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Considerations for prioritization of monitoring locations include: • Sociocultural value of sites. • Ecological value of sites. • Presence and status (stable, declining, lost) of bull kelp at a site. Monitoring both stable and declining/loss sites offers insight into factors affecting kelp status. • Connectivity/proximity with other monitoring sites (either ﬂoating kelp or environmental monitoring sites), and representativeness of environmental conditions and/or kelp persistence of a site within a region. • Management goals (e.g., priority area selection or monitoring) and co-location with other research, monitoring, and restoration projects. 4. Spatial extent and resolution This project included 15 core sites (Figure 1) throughout the US portion of the southern Salish Sea distributed at the widest spatial extent possible given practical limitations (Table 1).

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Site-level (i.e., a single monitoring location) is the only possible scale at which to collect most environmental data due to the cost and logistical difficulty of obtaining samples. However, site-level kelp bed area monitoring can be paired with region-wide kelp bed monitoring (e.g., WDNR’s high-resolution annual ﬁxed-wing aerial monitoring) and sitelevel environmental sensor data can inform larger-scale oceanographic modeling efforts (e.g., Salish Sea Model, Khangaonkar et al. 2017). These multi-scale datasets enable examination of the effects of spatial scale on the relationship between ﬂoating kelp and the environment, helping uncover processes at other non-monitored sites.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: The sites in this study were chosen to represent a range of ﬂoating kelp status (i.e., declining, lost, or stable), geography (i.e., Strait of Juan de Fuca, southern Strait of Georgia, San Juan Islands, and Puget Sound), and environmental characteristics (e.g., temperature gradient, proximity to the open ocean vs. estuarine habitat). Many of these 15 sites also already had a history of monitoring and data collection by the WA DNR kayak program (Ledbetter & Berry, 2025) and other programs and studies.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 10 Monitoring sites across a wide range of habitat conditions and kelp outcomes, including sites that represent the extreme ends of environmental gradients, provides the best chance of understanding the complex relationships between kelp persistence and environmental conditions. This requires both spreading sites across a large spatial gradient, when possible, to capture a wide range of habitat condition and oceanic inﬂuence, while also monitoring proximal sites with different kelp outcomes. For example, while Lincoln Park (LIP) and Wing Point (WNG), two sites in Central Puget Sound, are relatively close and experience similar conditions, LIP is stable while WNG has experienced a total loss of bull kelp.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: In contrast, Cherry Point (CHP), in northern Whatcom County, and Freshwater Bay (FWB), near Port Angeles on the Strait of Juan de Fuca, are far apart and experience different conditions but bull kelp appears stable at both. Additionally, this project did not conduct any environmental monitoring in the western Strait of Juan de Fuca or Olympic Coast due to capacity and travel constraints. However, these regions provide extensive habitat for kelp forests and should be monitored for changes in ﬂoating kelp presence and environmental conditions. They can serve as additional reference sites against which Salish Sea habitats can be compared. Limited sampling of bull kelp morphometrics and performance at Western Strait sites highlights salient differences between Puget Sound and more oceanic sites (Pﬁster et al. 2025; Pﬁster 2026).

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Continuing to monitor sites across a wide range of conditions and kelp outcomes and expanding to currently underrepresented areas will enable comparisons critical for understanding these systems. Consistent long-term monitoring of the same sites is essential because ecological and environmental conditions can vary substantially even between nearby locations that appear similar. Minor differences in depth, substrate, wave exposure, or freshwater inﬂuence can signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the biotic community, making nearby sites not interchangeable with one another. Repeatedly sampling the same sites allows observed changes to be more conﬁdently attributed to real temporal trends rather than differences in location. This consistency is particularly important for detecting gradual ecosystem change, evaluating disturbance and recovery, and distinguishing natural variability from long-term declines.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: The existing kelp bed area data collected by kelp kayak programs from WA DNR (Ledbetter & Berry, 2025), Samish Indian Nation DNR, and the Marine Resources Committees (MRC) provided a baseline of information which informed site selection for this project. Repeated monitoring at already-established sites would maintain and extend a valuable data record, to which new sites and/or monitoring methods could be added in the future. Due to the varied environmental conditions and kelp bed types in Washington, there is no “one-size-ﬁts-all” approach to choosing a method for ﬂoating kelp bed area monitoring. Different scales of surveys are required for different areas; for example, sites with sparse ﬂoating kelp require kayak or UAS surveys to adequately characterize bed area,

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 11 while sites with dense ﬂoating kelp may be characterized with kayak, UAS, or ﬁxed-wing aerial imagery. Large sites beneﬁt from the application of aerial imagery, especially when the kelp bed extends beyond an area that is reasonable to survey via kayak or UAS. Intentionally co-locating multiple scales of kelp bed survey methods at some sites will help clarify the differences in detection between methods and better inform interpretation of results in the context of resilience and loss.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Table 1 presents a list of sites studied in this project and considerations for their inclusion in continued monitoring. General recommendations are presented below. Recommendations: - Priority for foundational monitoring is to get broad coverage of a key set of parameters for understanding the system across a large spatial extent. For this purpose, we emphasize collecting basic information annually over an expansive network of sites, rather than intensive information over a small number of sites. - Continue regional-scale surface kelp bed monitoring efforts like WDNR’s highresolution annual ﬁxed-wing aerial monitoring program to extend insights gained from site-level monitoring to a wider area.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: - Continue and expand local-scale surface kelp bed monitoring efforts like the Marine Resources Committees (MRC) and WDNR kayak and UAS survey programs to identify status and trends at sites of interest (Table 1) at a ﬁner spatial resolution than can be captured with regional-scale kelp bed monitoring, especially in regions with few monitoring sites such as North Puget Sound and Admiralty Inlet. - Continue to utilize a variety of survey methods in a mosaic approach to map bed extent, where the extent and resolution of kelp bed area survey methods are matched with bed type and environmental conditions to provide the most accurate and useful mapping results. - Continue weaving together multiple data types and ways of knowing into the Floating Kelp Vital Sign Indicator.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: This includes using both regional- and local-scale kelp bed area monitoring efforts to calculate trends at nearly 200 locations in Washington currently reported on in the Indicator. - Establish additional environmental monitoring sites along the Western Strait of Juan de Fuca and the Olympic Coast. While these regions are well-surveyed by aerial monitoring efforts, they are currently underrepresenting in environmental monitoring and bull kelp morphometrics and conditions monitoring efforts, but they represent stable and substantial kelp forest habitat.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 14 5. Environmental monitoring This project collected a suite of environmental data at varied temporal resolutions for different parameters (Table 2). Benthic sensors were deployed continuously while singletime-point measurements were collected monthly for water quality parameters, and water samples were collected monthly for nutrient analyses. All environmental data for this project were collected from late 2023 through early 2025. This section presents considerations and recommendations for the collection of each parameter, based on the relative effort required to collect the data and the strength of the relationship between each parameter and kelp loss and resilience that this project found. Field and lab evidence suggests temperature is a primary parameter of concern for kelp loss and resilience, and this project found a strong correlation between high temperatures and kelp loss.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Temperature was collected for this project via both point measurements (data collection at a single time point) and continuous measurements. While point measurements can often provide more detailed information at the sampling time, continuously deployed sensors can measure the environment at depth over extended periods, capturing small scale (e.g., minutes to hours) temporal variability that would be missed by discrete sampling alone. This is particularly valuable in the context of temperature, where continuous sensors allow for the comparison of temperature trajectories over time between sites. For example, benthic sensors detected the highest temperatures at Squaxin Island in South Puget Sound and at Cherry Point in the southern Strait of Georgia. These sensors detected similar maximum temperatures at sites with different kelp outcomes;

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Squaxin Island has experienced major losses while Cherry Point appears to be stable. This indicates that maximum temperature alone cannot explain differences in kelp resilience. Using continuous benthic sensors, we detected a difference in thermal trajectories at Squaxin Island (consistent high temperatures throughout the summer) and Cherry Point (temperature peaks separated by substantially cooler periods). These trajectories were not detected in our monthly point measurements. This clearly demonstrates that continuous temperature sensors much more fully characterize thermal environments as compared to monthly sampling, which can result in powerful discrimination among thermal environments. As with temperature, salinity data was also collected via both point measurements and continuously deployed sensors.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: The capacity of point measurements to capture more detailed data throughout the water column was particularly valuable in the case of salinity. CTD casts capture vertical proﬁles of physical parameters throughout the water column, allowing researchers to determine features such as stratiﬁcation and mixed layer depth,

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 15 which may be linked to kelp loss. For example, CTD casts at Mukilteo, a site with recent kelp loss, revealed higher stratiﬁcation compared to other sites, likely associated with riverine freshwater input. While light is a key parameter for kelp growth, both continuous and single point light measurements (PAR) were expensive and difficult to collect, maintain, and analyze. Continuous light sensors fouled rapidly, and needed to be replaced frequently (e.g., at least quarterly) even though we used anti-fouling wipers. The equipment for single-point light proﬁles experienced frequent glitches and false readings, leading to the need to discard many data records.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Benthic PAR data were only useful for understanding light environments for ﬂoating kelp outside of the canopy season, since shading by the kelp itself alters the light environment and light levels at the benthos are less important for fully grown bull kelp. Additionally, Secchi depth, which can be collected as a point measurement, appears to provide qualitatively similar insight and is a less expensive and more reliable measurement method. While PAR data may provide insights into kelp loss and resilience, further targeted research and analysis effort is needed at this time to understand its utility at a broad scale. Nutrient limitation is emerging as a n important factor shaping bull kelp resilience, with nitrate concentrations being the most closely associated with bull kelp site status.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: For nitrate, the largest differences between site statuses occurred during the warmest months, when nitrate concentration fell to zero at multiple declining/lost sites. Nitrite and ammonium varied among months, but not between bull kelp site status; however, measuring both these nutrients allows calculation of total nitrogen and proportions of each nitrogen species, which may provide useful information about nutrient sources and dynamics. Continuing to monitor nitrogen, and particularly nitrate, will help ﬂag sites where nutrients are limiting bull kelp resilience. Further intensive studies could help elucidate complex nutrient dynamics and their relationship with bull kelp loss and resilience. Phosphate was not broadly limiting in this study, however two sites fell to near zero in June.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: This suggests that while phosphate measurements are not necessarily needed as part of broad-scale environmental monitoring, they may provide crucial information at certain sites. Additionally, simultaneous measurement of multiple nitrogen and phosphorus species at a higher sampling frequency may provide valuable insight into nutrient cycling processes and nutrient availability within bull kelp habitats. Silica varied seasonally, with March having higher concentrations at declining / lost sites and other months (i.e., July, September, October) having higher concentrations at stable sites. These dynamics are likely driven by phytoplankton blooms, and the magnitude of the

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 16 variability is likely shaped by temperature. Silica uptake by marine macroalgae increases with elevated temperatures, potentially providing protective beneﬁts in response to heat stress (Mizuta and Yasui, 2012). Since silica is not considered a limiting nutrient in this system (Bernhard and Peele, 1997), comprehensive broad-scale monitoring is likely unnecessary. However, targeted studies would improve our understanding of silica dynamics and their potential relationship to bull kelp resilience. TSS (total suspended solids) and POM (particulate organic matter) also varied seasonally, likely reﬂecting a combination of phytoplankton dynamics as well as riverine input. However, this study could not distinguish between the two drivers; 60% of POM samples were excluded because they fell below the minimum detection limit, removing multiple months during the winter when POM was low.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: These results suggest that a different collection and analysis protocol may be warranted to capture POM dynamics during nonpeak times. Additional sampling at ﬁner temporal scales (i.e., days to weeks) would help to capture transient phytoplankton blooms or brief freshwater events. In addition to monitoring frequency, the overall duration of data collection is a critical consideration. The new data collected for this project spanned 1 year of monitoring, constraining our insights into temporal environmental variability. Monitoring data become increasingly valuable as their temporal extent grows. As we build a longer library of environmental data at these key sites, we can better characterize expected conditions and ﬂag anomalies and potential stressful events.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Finally, collecting additional years of environmental data will allow direct comparisons with long-term trends and interannual variability in canopy extent and bed area. Recommendations: - Maintain continuous temperature monitoring at a broad range of sites. Temperature constitutes a key parameter for understanding kelp resilience and loss at a regional scale. Sites that experience periodic temperature extremes (e.g., Cherry Point) appear to perform differently than sites that experience sustained warming (e.g., Squaxin Island) (Cox et al. 2026b). Identifying thermal refugia and the different types of temperature trajectories that sites experience w ill contribute to understanding bull kelp vulnerability over time.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: - Conduct local intensive studies about nutrient cycling, temporal patterns in uptake and release, and relationship with bull kelp growth and performance to inform future monitoring efforts. Nutrient data are very likely to be an important parameter for kelp loss and resilience, and this work would be strengthened by partnerships with other monitoring programs (e.g., phytoplankton/zooplankton, stream ﬂow).

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 17 - Continue collecting Secchi depth and CTD casts concurrently with bull kelp kayak surveys, since these data provide useful environmental context for kelp observations, and are relatively easy to collect . Furthermore, collection of more frequent CTD proﬁles may be advisable for speciﬁc, short-term research questions such as characterizing the strength and duration of summer stratiﬁcation at sites of interest (e.g., Mukilteo and Edmonds). - Support other continuous environmental monitoring efforts such as Puget Sound Restoration Fund’s Eyes on Kelp Initiative, which has deployed a network of environmental monitoring buoy stations around the Salish Sea.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 20 6. Bull Kelp Distribution and Condition Monitoring This project collected data on various bull kelp distribution, morphometric, condition, and performance parameters at an annual frequency (once) at each site during summer, when ﬂoating kelp biomass was typically at its peak (Table 3, Table 4, Table 5). This frequency represents a minimum temporal resolution for these parameters. Kelp beds are highly dynamic, and sampling only once every few years would give low detection capability for capturing changes and trends. Timing data collection at the same time of year over multiple years provides the greatest likelihood that interannual and inter-site comparisons can be made appropriately. Bed area and depth distribution are two fundamental parameters that should be collected annually at all bull kelp monitoring sites.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: These two parameters provide basic understanding into what changes are occurring to the kelp bed, including spatial loss or expansion. Measuring kelp bed depth distribution (i.e., the range of depths where ﬂoating kelp occurs at an individual site) can identify if/when changes occur, such as shoaling of the deep edge, or deepening of the shallow edge of a bed. Identifying changes to bed depth distribution could help as early warning signs of potential stressors. Bed area data can be collected using multiple platforms (e.g., kayaks, drones, small boats, and small ﬁxed-wing aircraft), allowing for site-speciﬁc approaches based on resources and ﬁeld conditions. Bed area data can also be incorporated into the Washington State Floating Kelp Vital Sign Indicator (Berry et al. 2023), as long as consistent methods are developed and enough years of data are collected.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: For all of these reasons, we recommend that bed area and depth distribution be collected annually at ﬂoating kelp monitoring sites (Table 3). Collecting multiple kelp surveys per year during the growing season (‘seasonally’) would help to capture differences between beds or years for all parameters. Bull kelp bed phenology varies spatially through the southern Salish Sea, where beds closer to the Paciﬁc Ocean generally persist longer into the fall and even overwinter compared to those in further inland waters which are typically fully annual (McKenna, pers obs.). Since phenology also varies year-to-year with environmental and oceanic conditions, adding early (e.g., June) or late (e.g., September-October) bed area surveys to canopy-season bed area surveys (i.e., July- August), would help identify timing of initial bed growth and senescence.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Similarly, increased sampling frequency for kelp condition, morphometric, and performance parameters may also yield important insights given the seasonality of annual kelp growth and the temporal dynamics seen in the environmental data. Higherfrequency sampling for these parameters may be appropriate for local intensive studies with targeted questions.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 21 Recommendations: - Continue and expand annual surface kelp bed monitoring via regional-scale ﬁxedwing aerial monitoring and local-scale kayak monitoring using a mosaic approach (see Section II.4.); bed area and bed depth range are the most important measurements for annual monitoring , followed by density and/or canopy area. - Conduct site-level UAS monitoring at core sites annually and regional-scale UAS monitoring every several years in regions where ﬁxed-wing resolution is inadequate for kelp detection such as Central Puget Sound (McClure et al., 2025). - Select a few key morphometric, condition, and performance parameters to monitor annually across sites. While individual measures may be easy to collect, surveying all possible parameters is prohibitively intensive for routine monitoring across a large range of sites.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Priorities for basic morphometric, condition, and performance measurements are blade percent nitrogen, sub-bulb diameter, and reproductivity. Blade count, blade length, single-blade wet weight, mechanical damage, blade end fraying, and blade percent carbon can also provide valuable insight and are relatively easy to measure (Table 3). - Identify additional site-speciﬁc survey priorities. We emphasize that the prioritized lists (Tables 3-6) are generalized for annual surveys, and that speciﬁc research questions and/or focal sites may have different priorities. For example, targeted surveys of kelp crab abundance may be a priority at sites where populations seem to be disproportionately large (e.g., Squaxin Island), or sampling kelp performance at higher frequency may be important where nutrients limitations are a suspected stressor.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: - Conduct further targeted studies on physiological performance parameters such as blade carbon ﬁxation, nutrient uptake, DOC release, and others, particularly in areas where nutrient limitation is suspected based on data collected in this project, such as South and Central Puget Sound. Measures like percent tissue nitrogen could act as early warning systems to detect when low nutrient concentrations start affecting bull kelp physiology. While sampling effort makes performance parameters difficult to collect routinely at the scale of a large monitoring program, data collected throughout the growth and senescence period can provide valuable insight on nutrient dynamics which likely play an important role in bull kelp loss and resilience.

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 26 7. Benthic monitoring Benthic monitoring for this project (i.e., SCUBA surveys) identiﬁed a variety of physical characteristics as well as understory algae, invertebrate, and habitat assemblages (Table 6). Underwater surveys are useful for building a comprehensive understanding of the entire kelp forest ecosystem (Rubin et al. 2023; Freiwald et al. 2025). Benthic monitoring provides information on interspeciﬁc and intraspeciﬁc interactions, including those with allelopathic (e.g., Desmarestia) and invasive (e.g., Sargassum muticum) algae as well as trophic interactions with grazers such as kelp crabs (Pugettia spp.). Surveys of benthic characteristics (e.g., community assemblages, substrate surveys, sediment depth) can also provide information about the suitability of a site for potential bull kelp growth.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Reef Check Washington, a community-science monitoring group, conducts benthic surveys using SCUBA once per year at a growing list of sites, providing a snapshot of subtidal ecosystems where bull kelp is often present (Freiwald et al. 2025). As this dataset grows over time, it provides useful information about spatial and temporal changes at and among sites. Surveys conducted for this project used a modiﬁed version of Reef Check protocols at a more frequent survey interval (i.e., monthly or quarterly). Annual surveys are useful for assessing changes in the benthos over time, and more frequently repeated surveys (e.g., monthly during spring to summer) can answer questions about succession, interspeciﬁc and intraspeciﬁc competition, and recruitment throughout the growing season.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Concurrently with this study, another was conducted in which understory algae were cleared from the benthos and subsequent bull kelp recruitment was monitored (Fieber and Dethier, in prep). Manipulative in situ experiments such as this can provide valuable information on the dynamics of bull kelp ecosystems by answering targeted questions. Paired benthic and surface surveys (i.e. 3D swath) are needed in order to fully capture the abundance of grazers at sites where high abundances are suspected, or substantial mechanical damage is observed. Kelp crabs (Pugettia gracilis and P. producta), herbivores that eat kelp, were anomalously abundant near the water’s surface at one site (Squaxin Island), where bull kelp bulbs and blades had extensive mechanical damage such as scrapes and abrasions that appeared to be due to the kelp crabs.

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Benthic surveys did detect kelp crabs, but divers noted that since these crabs typically graze in the canopy, SCUBA-based counts of these species are likely to underestimate their impact. Benthic monitoring can also be accomplished with remotely operated vehicles (ROVs; Randell et al. 2024), towed underwater videography (e.g., Dowty et al. 2022), and other benthic photography and videography (e.g., video landers; WDNR Aquatic Reserves Program, dropcams; WDNR Aquatic Assessment and Monitoring Team). Each method has different

text: 29 Recommendations - Continue to support and collaborate with ongoing annual benthic monitoring programs such as Reef Check, USGS, Seattle Aquarium, and NOAA to continue building ecosystem-level understanding of bull kelp forests at sites throughout Washington State. - Utilize targeted benthic surveys to characterize understory algae communities and monitor their seasonal changes. Evidence suggests that bull kelp encounter interspeciﬁc competition with other benthic algae. Monitoring data from this study also indicate that several understory species rarely occur in areas without bull kelp, suggesting that certain understory kelps may indicate favorable conditions. - Utilize benthic monitoring to track bull kelp recruitment to understand recruitment timing (phenology). Bull kelp populations are often denser during early recruitment;

text: surveys at this stage provide information about juvenile attrition and can observe individuals that may not grow to reach the surface. - Conduct paired surveys (i.e., benthic and surface) to assess kelp crab populations and their effects on bull kelp at sites where high abundances are suspected, or substantial mechanical damage is observed. - Conduct benthic surveys to monitor the extent of soft substrates (i.e., sand), particularly at bull kelp sites near urbanized areas and/or freshwater inputs. ROV (e.g., Seattle Aquarium) or boat-based surveys (e.g., WDNR) could be used to cover targeted swaths of coastline and describe habitat suitability for bull kelp in these and other areas. - Create linkages with other benthic research; for example, use monitoring results to catalyze manipulative experiments to uncover mechanisms of resilience and loss.

text: 8. Data Processing and Analysis Support It is essential that, whichever combination of environmental, ecological, and physiological measurements are selected for monitoring, a plan is put into place to support long-term data processing, analysis, interpretation, and sharing. Optimizing data collection and carefully considering questions and goals are important, but without analysis capacity, that vital data may sit on a data sheet or hard drive, leaving questions unanswered. In a monitoring context, there is a large beneﬁt to investing in the development of robust data processing and analysis methods. The gains from such methods in efficiency, data quality, and data dissemination are compounded with the repeated cycles of data collection, processing, analysis and sharing. For example, the kelp bed area data collected for this project was relatively easy to process and analyze because protocols and scripts

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 30 had already been established through WDNR’s kayak monitoring program (Ledbetter & Berry 2025). However, each new environmental data stream collected for this project had to be quality controlled to exclude sensor errors and ensure that only accurate data were included. This required substantial effort, including the creation of processing scripts tailored to each sensor, as well as plotting scripts followed by manual review. Now that these methods and scripts are established, they can be maintained and used to increase efficiency of future monitoring data analysis. Continuing to invest time in the development of such data processing pipelines will help ensure that future years of monitoring data can be processed, analyzed, and disseminated efficiently.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: The data collected for the Bull Kelp Loss and Resilience project encompassed a wide range of parameters, both biological and environmental, collected at different intervals (e.g., continuous, monthly, seasonally, annually). Analyzing these datasets coherently with one another to generate insights and knowledge took signiﬁcant staff time, experience, and skill. For the project, we met approximately every other week with the project team , and we conducted one in-person data-sharing meeting with the core team. It was important that our meeting schedule was regular, but also ﬂexible – collaborators could join the meetings they were most interested in, and some meetings were canceled as necessary. These collaborative meetings accelerated analyses and interpretation and provided valuable insight.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: The monitoring recommendations proposed here will similarly generate highly varied data streams and datasets. While we do not recommend a rigid requirement for data-sharing meeting frequency, we do suggest that monitoring-based projects integrating multiple data sources across several collaborators include a tailored plan for how data sharing will be conducted throughout the duration of the project.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Recommendations: - Develop customized and reproducible data analysis protocols and processing pipelines such as developing/adapting scripts for data QA/QC, processing, analysis, and visualization. Any investment in the development of portable, reusable, and sharable scripts will pay dividends for future research and monitoring. - Budget staff time to support data management, analyses, distribution, and documentation. - Support data-sharing meetings, both regular check-ins with all data contributors and periodic in-person collaborative meetings to discuss data, hypotheses, and analyses. - Distribute data and documentation publicly via accessible platforms and data repositories such as WA Open Data Portal or Zenodo.

publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 31 - Allocate time for integration of monitoring data with existing data distribution and synthesis platforms such as the Floating Kelp Vital Sign and Floating Kelp Linear Extent Database (McKenna and Claar 2026). III. Conclusion During the Bull Kelp Resilience and Loss Project, teams conducted intensive environmental, biological, and ecological sampling at 15 sites over the course of a year (2024). The project examined patterns of bull kelp resilience and loss in relation to environmental conditions, benthic communities and composition, and bull kelp morphology, condition, and performance. The detailed monitoring highlighted the physical and biological differences between sites and emphasized the difficulty of understanding stressor response patterns at and among sites. While there were critical ﬁndings (see Claar et al., 2025a, Cox et al.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: 2026a, b, Dowty 2025, Fieber and Dethier 2026, Linhardt et al. 2026, and Pﬁster 2026), the one-year nature of the project limited the ability to capture and interpret longer-term patterns and identify speciﬁc causal factors for resilience or loss. To further understand and effectively manage ﬂoating kelp habitats for future generations, this report recommends establishing a tiered monitoring framework. This framework prioritizes essential kelp monitoring at a network of sites while allowing ﬂexibility to expand and address emerging research and management questions as capacity and funding allow by categorizing monitoring tasks into three tiers. Tier 1 tasks encompass basic, foundational monitoring tasks such as mapping kelp bed area. Tier 2 tasks help contextualize data collected by tier 1 tasks, adding signiﬁcant value to the baseline monitoring data.

title: Washington State Bull Kelp Strategic Monitoring Recommendations
publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
text: Tier 3 tasks are recommended for focused studies, developing new hypotheses, and/or piloting new data collection methods. Key recommendations based on these tiers include: • Continue annual surface monitoring of kelp beds at local and regional scales, • Expand monitoring to underrepresented regions that span a range of environmental conditions and management priorities, • Monitor key environmental conditions (Table 2) at core sites, • Support continued benthic surveys at sites throughout the regional, • Invest in data processing and analytical capacity, and • Support targeted, question-driven research. Together, these recommendations outline a practical and ﬂexible framework for multiorganizational monitoring of bull kelp forests in Washington State that balances scientiﬁc rigor with management relevance. By sustaining core long-term measurements, strategically expanding spatial and environmental coverage, and supporting targeted

text: 32 research to address key uncertainties, these recommendations aim to improve our collective ability to detect change, understand drivers of resilience and loss, and inform timely management actions. Continued investment in coordinated monitoring and data integration and sharing will be essential to conserve and restore kelp forests into the future. IV.
